analysis.one_liner: Hands the Tongass National Forest from federal to Alaska state control, with favorable terms for Alaska timber companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it drew zero cosponsors, got two field hearings in Alaska in July 1996, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have conveyed the entire Tongass National Forest — roughly 17 million acres of federal land in Southeast Alaska — to the State of Alaska, to be managed under state law instead of federal environmental rules. It also mandated that the state reinstate a specific pulp mill company's contract with the Forest Service and kill that company's lawsuit against the United States, and it repealed key protections from the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act and the Tongass Timber Reform Act. Logging and mining on the land would have run under Alaska's rules, with federal court review of the transfer largely stripped.
analysis.who_benefits: Alaska's timber industry gains the most: the bill requires the state to reinstate the Alaska Pulp Corporation's timber contract and dismiss its lawsuit against the United States [S3], requires the state to assume the Ketchikan Pulp Corporation contract [S3], and creates a timber road revolving fund seeded with federal stumpage revenue [S3]. Holders of federal mining claims keep 15-year rights to patent claims under federal law even after the land changes hands [S3]. The State of Alaska acquires the forest itself, along with the buildings, vehicles, and revenue from its timber [S3]. Five Alaska Native communities would receive surface land grants, with the subsurface estate going to Sealaska Corporation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill conveys all Tongass National Forest lands, structures, and operating property to Alaska automatically if the state elects to take them within 10 years, with the Secretary of Agriculture required to deliver the patent without conditions [S3].
It requires Alaska to reinstate the Alaska Pulp Corporation timber contract within six months of transfer and to secure dismissal of that company's pending lawsuit against the United States [S3].

It hands federal stumpage receipts from the Tongass to Alaska as seed money for a timber roads revolving fund, and allocates 25% of timber receipts to local boroughs and municipalities for schools and roads [S3].
It grants each of five Native communities 23,040 to 46,080 acres of surface estate, while conveying the subsurface rights beneath those lands to Sealaska Corporation [S3].
It preserves mining claim holders' rights to patent federal claims for 15 years after transfer and converts unpatented claims to state claims afterward [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The American public, which owns the Tongass, loses direct ownership and federal management of one of the nation's largest national forests. The bill repeals sections of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act and Title III of the Tongass Timber Reform Act on the transfer date [S3], and management would shift to Alaska law [S3]. The bill largely bars judicial review of the transfer in any U.S. court except in narrow cases [S3]. The United States would also remain on the hook for federal obligations during the transition period [S3], though Alaska would assume most obligations afterward [S3].

drawbacks.text: Transferring the forest to state management removes federal oversight and repeals Tongass-specific protections in ANILCA and the Tongass Timber Reform Act, shifting the land to a government whose bill findings emphasize timber and economic use [S3].

The bill writes a specific private benefit into law: reinstating one company's timber contract and extinguishing its lawsuit against the United States, with the state assuming the Forest Service's obligations under it [S3].

It bars judicial review of the transfer except in narrow constitutional or state-initiated cases, and declares that no formal rulemaking is needed to implement it, leaving affected parties limited recourse [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that transferring the forest would end the 25% federal revenue share to Alaska after 10 years and shift the full cost of managing roads, fires, and fish and wildlife programs to Alaska taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Alaska and its timber communities would gain direct control of land, revenue, and jobs, and the Native land grants address real unmet claims from the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act. But the core trade is handing a national forest belonging to all Americans to a single state, under rules written to favor large timber contract holders and mining claimants, with court challenges essentially shut off. The timber and mining provisions, not the land grants or local school funding, are the bill's center of gravity.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, and the sponsor held two field hearings in Alaska in the summer of 1996, but it was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on September 28, 1995, and it was referred to the House Resources Committee and the House Agriculture Committee [S1] [S5].

In October 1995 it was referred to the Agriculture Committee's Resource Conservation, Research and Forestry Subcommittee, and executive comment was requested from the USDA and Interior Department [S5].
Field hearings were held in Sitka on July 3, 1996 and Thorne Bay on July 5, 1996, and the sponsor gave introductory remarks several more times through 1996 [S5].
The bill never received a markup or a floor vote in either chamber and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The American public kept the Tongass under federal ownership and management. Alaska's large pulp and timber companies did not get their contracts reinstated or their lawsuits dismissed through legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and there were no votes, so no partisan lineup ever formed on the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would reinstate the Alaska Pulp Corporation's federal timber contract, extinguish its lawsuit against the United States, and shift the Ketchikan Pulp contract to the state, all backed by a federal stumpage-funded road program. These companies profit from logging publicly owned forest at below full public cost, and the bill locks in their role before the land even changes hands.

industries.industry: Mining claim holders in the Tongass
industries.note: Claimants would keep 15 years of federal patent rights after transfer and convert claims to state claims on favorable terms, extracting hard-rock minerals from what is now a national forest under 1872 Mining Law terms that give the public little return.

The bill routes the subsurface estate of new Native community land grants to Sealaska. The surface grants serve unmet Native land claims, but the subsurface conveyance directs timber and mineral value to the regional corporation.

industries.industry: U.S. Forest Service operations and forest products users nationwide
industries.note: Federal ownership of the Tongass ends, along with the federal 25% revenue share to states and the national forest system's largest unit; the public's access and oversight would run through Alaska state law instead.
